title: The Giant Panda
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The giant panda is one of the most easily recognised animals in the world, with its round face, black patches around the eyes and thick black-and-white coat. It lives in a few mountain forests in central China, in the provinces of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, at heights of between 1,200 and 3,400 metres. Pandas have become the symbol of the World Wide Fund for Nature, and the sight of one chewing bamboo can attract crowds of visitors to zoos in many countries of the world. Its slow, gentle manner and its habit of sitting upright to eat make it especially appealing to children, and baby pandas are among the most popular animals ever filmed.

Although pandas belong to the group of animals known as carnivores, which includes bears, cats and dogs, their diet consists almost entirely of bamboo. A panda eats between twelve and thirty-eight kilograms of it each day, and spends about twelve hours a day feeding. Because bamboo gives little nourishment, and the panda's digestive system is better suited to meat, it must eat huge amounts. Pandas have a special adaptation: a bone in the wrist, called the false thumb, which they use to hold the stalks.

Pandas are solitary animals. Each adult has its own territory, which it marks with scent from glands under its tail, and it avoids contact with others except during the breeding season in spring. Female pandas can have babies only once every two years, and they usually give birth to one or two cubs. A newborn cub is tiny, weighing about one hundred grams, which is roughly a thousandth of its mother's weight, and it is blind, pink and almost hairless.

If two cubs are born, the mother usually raises only one, because she cannot find enough food for both. The cub opens its eyes at about six to eight weeks, and begins to crawl after three months. It stays with its mother for about eighteen months to two years, learning which bamboo to eat and how to climb trees. Cubs are very playful and spend much of their time wrestling with each other and rolling down slopes, which scientists believe helps to develop strong muscles.

During the twentieth century, the panda's population fell dangerously. The forests where it lives were cut down for farmland and for timber, and the bamboo itself periodically flowers and dies, which leaves pandas without food unless they can move to another area. In the 1980s, the number of wild pandas fell to about 1,100. China responded by creating a network of nature reserves, planting bamboo corridors between forests, and banning hunting and logging.

The effort has been successful. A survey in 2014 counted 1,864 pandas in the wild, and in 2016 the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which keeps the record of threatened species, changed the panda's status from 'endangered' to 'vulnerable'. Zoos have contributed by learning how to breed pandas in captivity, a task that was long thought to be impossible. Some captive-bred animals have been released into the forests, but a good deal of care is needed to prepare them. Scientists teach the young animals to find food and to avoid people before they leave the breeding centre, and they track them afterwards with collars that send signals to satellites.

Nevertheless, the future of the panda is not secure. Climate change may reduce the area of bamboo by a third in the next eighty years, and roads and dams divide the forests into smaller pieces, so that pandas cannot find mates. Dr Wei Zhang, a conservation biologist, says that protecting the panda also protects thousands of other species that share its forest, which is why the animal is sometimes called an umbrella species. The panda thus matters far more than its charm alone would suggest.
